turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Mr. Keene, come on back, please. Before Dr. Ellison comes in, I have your medication list up, and it shows ibuprofen eight hundred milligrams by mouth twice a day. I wanted to check that with you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning. Thank you. I am afraid that is not quite right. I take four hundred milligrams by mouth, twice a day, and I never started the eight hundred.

[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll flag the mismatch. Just now your blood pressure was one thirty-eight over eighty-four, your pulse was seventy-six, and the scale read one hundred ninety-two pounds.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, that is helpful. The blood pressure sounds like what I usually hear. I did have a little trouble finding parking on the second level, so I am glad you called me back promptly.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mr. Keene, I'm Dr. Ellison. The chart has you at fifty-four. Thanks for waiting. What brought you in today?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you for seeing me, doctor. It is my lower back. It has been aching, and I felt I should have it looked at properly rather than keep guessing.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you came in. When did the aching start?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): That I cannot date cleanly, and I apologize. It has been a few weeks, or perhaps since the move. The move was late summer, but whether the end of August or into September, I truly cannot say.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): So a few weeks, linked in your mind to the move, and the actual date stays fuzzy. I won't pin a calendar day on it. Where do you feel the pain?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Across the low back, well, central at first thought, but actually a little more on the right, these past few weeks. Most of the time it is a dull ache. If I bend to pick something up, it catches, sharp, just for a second.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dull ache, right low back, with a sharp catch on bending. What is your work like day to day?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I am an office manager at a parts warehouse. Most of the day I am at a desk, though we have been short-handed, so I have been lifting cartons as well. The household move added quite a lot of that.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Desk work, plus extra lifting at the warehouse and during the move. What makes it worse, and what gives you any relief?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): A long meeting, sitting, makes it worse, and so does lifting. Lying flat on the floor for a little while helps. The ibuprofen takes the edge off, though not completely.

[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me reflect the medicine piece before we leave it. The list says eight hundred milligrams twice a day, and you said four hundred. What do you actually swallow, and how often?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Four hundred milligrams, by mouth, twice a day, with food. I am quite sure of the four hundred. Some evenings I do forget the second dose, so I would not claim I am perfectly regular.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right. You take four hundred, the chart says eight hundred, the plan on paper is twice a day, and some evening doses get missed. Any other pain medicine at all?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. I have used a heating pad in the evening. Nothing else from the pharmacy. My brother offered me one of his old muscle pills, and I declined it.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good that you didn't take someone else's pills. Any numbness or tingling in the legs?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. I would not say so. The pain stays in the back.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with the bladder, trouble starting the urine, or any leaking?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing of that sort. It has been entirely normal.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight without trying?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not believe so. My trousers fit as they did in the spring. My wife said I looked thinner after the move, but that was a new belt, I think, and I have not seen the home scale change in any way I could swear to.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, chills, or feeling ill along with the pain?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I did sweat a great deal the afternoon we moved the sofa, but the air conditioning was not connected yet, so I took it for the heat. It was not an illness, as far as I could tell.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weakness in either leg, or pain that shoots down past the knee?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness. It does not travel down the leg. I can still walk my usual loop around the block after dinner.

[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Low back pain for a few weeks or since the move, date unclear, worse with sitting and lifting, a bit better lying down, ibuprofen helps some, no bladder change, no weight loss, no fever, no weakness, no pain down the leg. Is that complete?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): That is fair, doctor. Well, actually, I should correct the numbness, because I dismissed it too quickly. The outside of my left thigh gets tingly, almost numb, if I drive more than about twenty minutes. It fades once I step out and walk a little.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you. So the outer left thigh tingles or goes nearly numb on longer drives, and it clears when you walk. It is not there all the time.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. Not constant. I am sorry I said no at first. I had put it down to the car seat, and that was too quick of me.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): No apology needed. I would rather have the correction. Has anyone imaged this back before?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Some years ago they did an X-ray of the low back, though I cannot tell you the year, last winter or the one before. They said it was borderline, something about the disc space, I think, and they did not treat it. I did not keep the paper.

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): An old low-back X-ray, the year unclear, described to you as borderline, maybe the disc space, with no treatment afterward. I will not treat the word borderline as a real measurement. Any surgery on the back, or surgery of any kind?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none. I have never had an operation.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any ongoing conditions, high blood pressure, diabetes, anything you are followed for?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. I have been fortunate in that respect. There is nothing ongoing, and I am not being treated for blood pressure or diabetes.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines, foods, anything?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I know of.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or drink alcohol regularly?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I take a glass of wine with dinner now and then, perhaps two evenings in a week. Nothing beyond that.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): And at home, who is in the apartment with you? I ask because of the move you mentioned.

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): My wife and I. It is a second-floor place. I mention the stairs only because they do stir the back a little, not to complain about the building. The neighbors have been perfectly kind.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you. I'd like to examine your back now, if you are agreeable. I'll tell you what I'm doing as I go.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course, doctor. Please go ahead.

[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): There is tenderness over the right lower lumbar muscles, and none over the midline bone. Bending forward is limited by pain, roughly two thirds of what I would expect. Straight leg raise is negative on both sides, leg strength is full, and the skin sensation on that thigh is intact while you are lying here.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): The thigh feels quite ordinary at the moment. It really is only in the car, as I said.

[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): That pattern fits something positional, not a fixed numb patch. I'm going to call this mechanical low back pain, most likely a strain from the lifting and the move. I can't fully set aside a little nerve irritation, given the thigh symptom with driving, but nothing I see today looks like an emergency.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I appreciate you putting it so plainly.

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): On the ibuprofen, I won't write a new strength over a disagreement. Keep taking the four hundred milligrams twice a day with food, since that is what you are actually using, and try not to skip the evening one when the pain is up. If your stomach burns, stop it and call us, and we will have the pharmacy reconcile the eight hundred still sitting on the list.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I will do that. My stomach has been fine with it, for what it is worth. I take it after breakfast and, when I remember, after dinner.

[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stay as active as the pain allows, short walks rather than bed rest. Hold off on lifting those cartons for now, take the stairs one at a time if you need them, and the heating pad is fine.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I can speak with the warehouse about the lifting. It will help to have a clear instruction to pass along. I would not want to simply disappear from the floor without a reason.

[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the pain is not clearly settling in about four weeks, or if the thigh numbness becomes constant, or you develop bladder trouble, weakness, fever, or weight loss you can't explain, then we should get imaging. I am not ordering an X-ray or an MRI today.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems measured. I would rather not have a test I do not need. Um, if I may ask, is walking the block still all right?
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, walking is all right, and I'd like to see you back in three weeks either way, to check the pain and that thigh symptom. Don't wait on me to decide about the walking.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks is very manageable. Should I call sooner if something changes, rather than wait?
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. If the numbness stops fading after you walk, call us. If you cannot pass urine at all, don't wait for the visit, go to the emergency room the same day.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand, and I will not wait if that occurs. You have been very clear.
[SEG0061] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry to lean in, Dr. Ellison. Do you want the three-week visit booked before he goes, and should I send the ibuprofen mismatch over to the pharmacy window?

[SEG0062] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, please book three weeks with me, late morning if you can. And yes, send the discrepancy so they can confirm which strength is on the active prescription. I don't want to guess between four hundred and eight hundred.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you both. One small thing, if I may. Should I try to find that old report, the one they called borderline?
[SEG0064] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you come across it, bring it next time. It would help, but don't delay anything hunting through boxes. And again, I am not taking borderline as a figure we can act on.

[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): I will look. I cannot promise the paper survived the move. It really might have been the winter before last. I simply do not know, and I don't want to invent a year for you.

[SEG0066] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's all right. Let me set the plan out once more. Continue four hundred milligrams of ibuprofen twice a day with food, with the chart still saying eight hundred until the pharmacy checks. Activity as tolerated, no heavy lifting, back here in three weeks, and imaging only if this is not settling in about four weeks or a red flag shows up.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. That matches what I heard. I am grateful for the time you have given me.

[SEG0068] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): You're booked for three weeks from today, late morning. I'll take the ibuprofen note to the pharmacy window before you leave. You can wait by the front chairs if you like, they're quieter than the hallway.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Late morning suits me very well. Thank you. I will wait where you said.
[SEG0070] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mind the stairs on your way out, Mr. Keene. We'll go over whatever the pharmacy says when I see you next.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): I will be careful. Good day, doctor, and thank you again.
[SEG0072] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): You're all set. Right this way, Mr. Keene.

spec.situation: Manual worker or office worker with low back pain for 'a few weeks or since the move'; doctor asks about red flags (numbness, bladder, weight loss, fever) one by one; patient answers some clearly, some vaguely or with a story. Painkiller use mentioned.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

bad.reason: Patient says he does not believe so, not a definite negative.
